summary: Describes how to generate an authentication tag using UMAC, a message authentication code designed to be very fast in software. It applies a universal hash function to the message and key, then combines the result with a pseudorandom pad made using a block cipher. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A quick way to stamp a message with a secret seal so anyone with the secret can tell it was not changed.

questions: when to use umac for authentication
umac tag length and forgery probability
subtitle: A fast, provably-secure message authentication code using universal hashing.

tldr.problem: Applications need message authentication that is both very fast in software and mathematically proven secure. Standard MACs can be slow, and high-speed MACs often lack rigorous security proofs.
tldr.mechanism: UMAC applies a universal hash function to the message, producing a short fixed-length value, then masks it by XORing with a key-derived pseudorandom pad. The result is an authentication tag that proves the message has not been modified.
tldr.outcome: UMAC achieves speeds of about one CPU cycle per byte on modern processors while offering provable security guarantees. It remains an efficient and trusted choice for high-performance message authentication.

facts.label: Peak performance
facts.value: One CPU cycle per byte on modern processors

today: RFC 4418 is an Internet Standard specification for UMAC. It has not been obsoleted, updated, or superseded, and remains the current definition of the UMAC algorithm.

sections.title: What UMAC Is
sections.content:
UMAC stands for Universal Message Authentication Code. It is a cryptographic algorithm that creates a short authentication tag for a message, proving that only someone with the secret key could have generated it. Unlike older encryption-based MACs, UMAC is designed to be extremely fast to compute in software on standard processors.

UMAC is based on Wegman-Carter authentication, a well-studied approach that combines a fast universal hash function with a pseudorandom pad. The basic formula is simple: the tag is computed as the XOR of a hashed message and a random pad derived from the key and a nonce. The security of UMAC has been rigorously analyzed and proven in peer-reviewed academic papers.
sections.plainLanguage: UMAC is like a special security stamp you put on a message with a secret key. Anyone with the key can verify the stamp matches, but without the key, no one can forge it or even know if the message changed.

sections.title: How UMAC Works
sections.content:
UMAC generates a tag in three steps. First, it applies a function called UHASH to the message and a secret key, producing a hash output of 4, 8, 12, or 16 bytes depending on the desired security level. Second, it generates a pseudorandom pad using the key and a nonce (a value used once per message). Third, it XORs the hash output with the pad to produce the final authentication tag.

A nonce is essential: no two messages under the same key can use the same nonce, or security is lost. The nonce does not need to be secret, only unique. In practice, it can be a counter that increments with each message, a random value, or a sequence number from the transport protocol.

UMAC can produce four variants: UMAC-32, UMAC-64, UMAC-96, and UMAC-128, generating 32-, 64-, 96-, or 128-bit tags respectively. Longer tags offer stronger security at the cost of slightly more computation.
sections.plainLanguage: UMAC takes your message and secret key, scrambles them together to get a short number, then masks that number with a random pad. The result is your authentication tag. Each message needs a different random pad.

sections.title: The Universal Hash Function
sections.content:
UHASH, the core of UMAC, is a three-layer hash function designed for speed. The first layer, L1-HASH, breaks the message into 1024-byte chunks and applies a high-speed operation called NH that multiplies and adds 32-bit words together. This reduces very long messages to much shorter outputs quickly.

The second layer, L2-HASH, is a polynomial hash over the L1 output. If the message is short (under 1024 bytes), L2-HASH is skipped as an optimization. The polynomial hash uses prime-modulus arithmetic to ensure mathematical security guarantees.

The third layer, L3-HASH, reduces the 16-byte output of L2 down to 4 bytes through an inner-product calculation modulo a prime. Multiple iterations of the three-layer process are concatenated if the desired output is longer than 4 bytes.

This multi-layer design balances speed with the mathematical properties needed for provable security. The universal hash property means that, for any two different inputs, the probability that L1 and L3 produce the same output is very small, a property essential to Wegman-Carter authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: UHASH works in three stages. First, it quickly breaks a long message into chunks and combines them. Second, if needed, it does a fancy number trick to mix everything together. Third, it shrinks the result down to the right size. Each stage is designed to be fast and mathematically trustworthy.

sections.title: Security Guarantees
sections.content:
UMAC's security is proven in academic papers using standard cryptographic assumptions. The core UHASH function is proven to have collision resistance regardless of cryptographic advances: the probability of two different inputs producing the same hash is bounded purely by mathematics, not by assumptions about how hard it is to break a cipher.

When UMAC is instantiated with truly random keys and pads, the probability of forging a tag for UMAC-32, UMAC-64, UMAC-96, or UMAC-128 is at most 1/2^30, 1/2^60, 1/2^90, or 1/2^120 respectively. In the actual specification, AES (the Advanced Encryption Standard) is used to generate the pseudorandom material. As long as AES is secure, these bounds increase only by a negligible amount related to AES security.

The RFC warns of several important considerations. Repeating a nonce with the same key destroys security; the receiver should check that nonces never repeat. Tag-prefix verification (accepting part of a tag as valid) is dangerous and can reduce security to the verified length. Side-channel attacks, such as timing attacks, are possible if the POLY algorithm is not implemented carefully to take equal time regardless of input values.
sections.plainLanguage: Mathematicians have proven that UMAC is very hard to forge: even with a computer trying billions of times, the odds of guessing a valid tag are astronomically small. But you must never use the same nonce twice with the same key, or the proof breaks.

sections.title: Performance and Implementation
sections.content:
UMAC is designed for high performance. On an Intel Pentium 4 with SSE2 instructions, UMAC processes 64-bit tags at about one CPU cycle per byte for messages around four kilobytes or longer. On a Pentium III without SSE2 parallelism, the rate is about two cycles per byte. For shorter messages, performance is still good: around four cycles per byte on 256-byte messages and under two cycles per byte on 1500-byte messages.

The time to produce shorter tags is proportionally faster: 32-bit tags take roughly half the time of 64-bit tags. The RFC includes test vectors showing UMAC outputs for various input lengths and tag sizes, allowing implementers to verify their implementations.

UMAC requires only addition and multiplication of 32-bit and 64-bit integers, operations efficiently supported by contemporary processors. The RFC specifies AES as the default block cipher for generating keys and pads, though other block ciphers with 16-byte blocks can be substituted by agreement of the communicating parties.
sections.plainLanguage: UMAC is so fast because it uses simple math that modern computers are really good at: adding and multiplying small numbers. The speed depends on the message length and which variant you use, but it is much faster than older authentication methods.

sections.title: Status
sections.content: RFC 4418 is an Informational RFC published in March 2006. It remains the canonical specification for UMAC and has not been obsoleted or updated. The RFC is widely trusted in the cryptography and security communities.
sections.plainLanguage: UMAC is still the standard way to do fast authentication. No newer version has replaced it.
